text:
A corn kernel is made up of the fruit wall/pericarp (seed coat), the endosperm (the starchy food reserve, roughly 90% of the kernel), and the embryo, which together make the kernel a good source of vitamins A, E, and B-group vitamins as well as minerals.

Germination begins with the radicle (root) emerging from the kernel, growing downward into the soil, while the coleoptile -- a protective sheath around the young shoot -- pushes upward. Once the coleoptile reaches the soil surface, it stops elongating and the first true leaf emerges through it. Under good soil moisture and temperature, emergence typically takes about 5-7 days from planting, though cold or crusted soil, or seed planted too deep or too shallow, can delay or prevent even emergence.

As the seedling establishes, temporary seminal roots from the seed are progressively replaced by a permanent nodal (crown) root system that develops from the lower stem nodes; later in the season, above-ground brace (prop) roots also develop from the nodes near the base of the stalk, providing extra anchorage and nutrient/water uptake as the plant grows tall and top-heavy.
